Writing about conditions rather than people is both the more transferable account and the one that keeps the next report coming.
questions.mindset: Write up a failure so that the next person is willing to report theirs.

questions.stem: Your squad is the third team in eighteen months to discover that the shared identity service silently truncates long email addresses. Each team found it the same way, lost about a week, and recorded it in its own retrospective. The service belongs to a platform group that does not attend your reviews and whose backlog you cannot see. Your squad's position is that this is not their problem to solve. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Get the finding into the platform group's own intake, and pursue the defect being fixed rather than the discovery being recorded.
options.rationale: Three retrospectives have already demonstrated that recording it locally changes nothing. The only place the knowledge does any work is with the people who can remove the cause.

options.text: Write it up for the organisation's lessons repository so the next team finds it before starting.
options.rationale: The repository has now failed twice against this exact defect. It also assumes the next team searches for a problem it does not yet know exists, which is the assumption the evidence contradicts.

options.text: Warn the other squads directly so that nobody loses a week to it again.
options.rationale: It inoculates the teams that exist today and leaves the defect in place, so the cost simply returns with the next squad or the next joiner. Person-to-person warning does not scale past the people you happen to know.

options.text: Document the workaround in your squad's codebase and move on.
options.rationale: It resolves the issue for one team at the price of three more discoveries, and it is the option the squad's own view of ownership points to. Being right that it is not your defect does not make it cheaper for the organisation.

questions.explanation: Repeated rediscovery of the same problem is evidence that the routing of knowledge has failed, not that people are recording too little. Knowledge reaches its destination when it lands with an owner able to act on it, and a repository that no one queries before they have the problem is not such a destination. Where the knowledge is really about a defect, the durable form of transfer is removing the thing being learned about, which is a harder ask across a team boundary and the only one that ends the recurrence.
questions.mindset: Route what you learn to whoever can remove the cause, not to wherever it is easiest to file.

questions.stem: Six weeks ago your squad handed the member portal to a pension administrator's permanent product team. Three things have happened since, each pulling one of your developers back in, and each needs a different response if the handover is to hold. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A member of the new team messages your developer directly for the fourth time this week with a routine question already covered in the handover. Your developer should
The new team hits a failure mode nobody anticipated and has no starting point for diagnosing it. Your developer should
The new team asks for a reporting change they are capable of making themselves but have not attempted. Your developer should

options.text: answer it once, then help them put the answer where their own team will look for it next time
options.rationale: Refusing damages the relationship and answering repeatedly entrenches the dependency, so the useful move is to answer and simultaneously remove the reason to ask again. Recurrence is the signal that something is missing from their material, not that they are lazy.

options.text: work it through with them and treat the gap as something the handover missed
options.rationale: A genuinely novel failure is outside what any handover could have covered, so this is legitimate support rather than backsliding. Recording it as a gap is what stops the next one being handled the same way by default.

options.text: talk them through making the change themselves rather than making it for them
options.rationale: They have the capability and lack the confidence, so doing it for them removes the one opportunity to establish it. The time cost is similar and only one version leaves them able to do the next one.

options.text: redirect them to their own team lead and decline to engage
options.rationale: Not used. A flat redirect ends the contact without transferring anything, and its real effect is that the next question does not get asked at all. Unasked questions become defects rather than disappearing.

questions.explanation: After a handover the receiving team will keep making contact, and the response has to distinguish between a question that reveals a gap in the handover, one that reveals a gap in confidence, and one that is simply easier to ask than to look up. Each has a different remedy, and treating them all as backsliding to be refused ends the contact rather than the dependency. The general test is whether the response leaves the receiving team more able to handle the next instance without you.
questions.mindset: Answer in the way that makes the next question unnecessary rather than unwelcome.

questions.stem: A highways depot holds 48 winter-service procedures. A review finds 30 have been verified within the last twelve months and the rest have not been looked at since. Your project changes how gritting routes are planned, and you have agreed with the depot manager that the whole set will be current before next winter, six months away. Work out the size of the task and how to sequence it.

blanks.label: Percentage of the 48 procedures currently verified, to the nearest whole number
blanks.rationale: 30 of 48 is 62.5%, which rounds to 63%. Stating it as a proportion is what makes the position arguable with a depot manager who believes the set is broadly fine.

blanks.label: Number of procedures that must be verified each month to clear the backlog in six months
blanks.rationale: Eighteen unverified procedures over six months is three a month. Expressing the backlog as a monthly rate turns an intimidating total into a commitment somebody can actually accept.

blanks.label: Which should be verified first — the ones your project changes, or the ones that are oldest
accept: the ones changed by the project
the ones affected by the project
blanks.rationale: Age is a proxy for risk; being changed by live work is direct evidence of it. A procedure your project is altering is certain to be wrong the day the change lands, whereas an old one may still be perfectly accurate.

questions.explanation: Documentation currency is manageable only when it is measured, because an unmeasured set drifts until people stop trusting all of it. Converting a backlog into a monthly rate makes it a commitment somebody can own rather than a project nobody starts. Sequencing should follow evidence of inaccuracy rather than age, since the procedures your own work is changing are guaranteed to be wrong on a known date while an old procedure may never have needed to change at all.
questions.mindset: Measure how much of the record is current, then work the backlog at a rate somebody can own.

questions.stem: Your desalination plant control upgrade closes next month. Three things the project has produced will outlive it, and each will only be found later if it is lodged with the group that maintains that kind of material. Getting this wrong is not visible at closure and becomes visible years afterwards. Match each to the home it should have. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The tested sequence for restarting the reverse-osmosis trains after an unplanned power loss.
The finding that running two commissioning stages in parallel cost more than the four weeks it saved.
The correspondence establishing what the supplier warranted about membrane life and on what conditions.

options.text: The plant's operating procedure set, owned by the operations manager
options.rationale: It will be needed at short notice by whoever is on shift, so it has to sit where operators already look under pressure. It also needs an owner who will keep it current as the plant changes.

options.text: The organisation's lessons repository, with the supporting evidence attached
options.rationale: This is a finding about how to run projects rather than how to run a plant, so its readers are future project teams. Without the evidence it reads as an opinion and will be discounted by anyone who prefers the parallel approach.

options.text: The contract file held by the commercial team
options.rationale: A warranty is only enforceable if its conditions can be produced years later by people who were not there. The commercial team is the group that retains such material and gets asked for it when a claim arises.

options.text: The project's own closure report
options.rationale: Not used. A closure report is read once, by people confirming the project ended properly, and then filed by project rather than by subject. Anything placed there is effectively lost to everyone searching by topic later.

questions.explanation: At closure the question for every durable artefact is who will come looking for it, and in what circumstances, because that determines which custodian should hold it. Material filed by project rather than by subject is retrievable only by someone who already knows which project produced it, which is exactly what a future searcher does not know. The instinct to consolidate everything into one comprehensive closure document optimises for the closing team and defeats every later reader.
questions.mindset: File what outlives the project where its future reader will look, not where the project would file it.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the path a fault takes through your parcel carrier's support arrangements after the new depot scanning system went live eight weeks ago. Around seventy per cent of the faults now reaching the project team are ones second line was trained and equipped to resolve, and second line is passing them on within minutes of receipt. Select the point in the path where the knowledge transfer has failed.

graphic.title: Fault escalation path from depot user through first and second line to the project team
graphic.caption: Select a point in the path. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between points, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Depot user raises the fault
regions.rationale: Depot users are raising faults through the route they were given, and nothing in the figures suggests they are reporting badly. Volume arriving at the far end says nothing about how it entered.

regions.label: First line records and triages
regions.rationale: First line is passing faults to second line, which is what triage is supposed to do with anything technical. It is a natural pick for anyone who assumes the earliest tier is where filtering breaks down.

regions.label: Second line, trained on these faults, forwards them on
regions.rationale: This is the tier that was trained, equipped and expected to resolve these faults and is not doing so. Passing them on within minutes shows they are not being attempted, which points to capability or confidence rather than difficulty.

regions.label: Project team resolves and returns the fix
regions.rationale: This is where the consequence lands and is therefore the most visible point, but the project team is doing exactly what an escalation of last resort should do. Mistaking where a problem is measured for where it is caused is the usual error with escalation data.

questions.explanation: An escalation path shows where work is arriving, and the failure sits at the last tier that should have stopped it and did not. The distinguishing evidence is what that tier was expected to handle compared with what it actually attempts, which is why the speed of the pass-on matters as much as the volume. Reading the pain point as the failure point puts effort into the group that is already coping and leaves the untested tier untouched.
questions.mindset: Look for the failure at the last point that should have handled it, not the point where it hurts.

questions.stem: The engineering wiki for an equipment hire firm's booking product has grown to around 1,400 pages over four years. New joiners say they cannot tell which pages are current, and the experienced developers have stopped using it altogether, keeping personal notes instead. Any proposal to delete anything makes people uneasy, and the last attempt stalled. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Identify the small set of pages that answer the questions people actually ask, and give each a named owner accountable for it being right.
options.rationale: Starting from real questions finds the fraction that carries almost all the value, and an owner is what keeps a page trustworthy afterwards. Without ownership the curated set decays back into the same condition.

options.text: Move everything unread in a year into a clearly marked archive rather than deleting it, so the working set becomes small.
options.rationale: The obstacle is fear of losing something, and archiving addresses that directly at almost no cost. It shrinks what a reader has to judge without requiring anyone to certify that a page is worthless.

options.text: Delete every page not updated within the last twelve months.
options.rationale: Update date is a weak proxy for value, since a good page describing something stable needs no edits. It is also the proposal that has already stalled once, because irreversibility is what people object to.

options.text: Ask every author to review the pages they wrote.
options.rationale: Many authors have left over four years, and those remaining are the developers who have stopped using the wiki. It distributes the work to precisely the people least motivated and least available to do it.

options.text: Add a banner to each page showing when it was last updated.
options.rationale: It makes staleness visible without reducing it, leaving the reader to judge 1,400 pages instead of the system doing the judging. Effort that improves the display of a problem rather than its size.

questions.explanation: A knowledge base fails on findability long before it fails on content, and past a certain size adding material makes it less useful rather than more. Recovering it means shrinking the working set to what demand actually justifies and attaching ownership so trust can be rebuilt, since an unowned page cannot be relied on however good it was when written. Reversible moves such as archiving get past the loss aversion that stalls every deletion proposal.
questions.mindset: Curate down to what people ask for and give it an owner, because an unowned page cannot be trusted.
